title: Ravana rides out

segments.voice: Yesterday: Kumbhakarna wakes, the giant who told his brother the truth and fought for him anyway.

For the whole war, Ravana has sent other people. Generals. Sons. His giant brother. One by one, they've fallen. Kumbhakarna is gone. Now even Indrajit, his great son, the master of illusion, has been killed by Lakshmana. There's nobody left to send. So the king of Lanka puts on his armor, climbs into his chariot, and rides out through the gates himself. Ten heads. Twenty arms. A bow in several hands at once. After all these weeks, the serial brings the two of them face to face: Rama on foot, Ravana in the chariot.
screen: `EVERYONE HE SENT HAS FALLEN.` → `THE GATES OPEN.` → `FACE TO FACE, AT LAST.`

segments.voice: It's easy to make Ravana a cartoon, and the Ramayana doesn't. In the tradition he's a great scholar, learned in the Vedas, and a fierce devotee of Shiva; a hymn to Shiva's dance, the Shiva Tandava Stotram, is traditionally said to be his. Tradition makes him a veena player too. He's brave, and a real king to his people. And he took another man's wife by force and wouldn't give her back when everyone he trusted begged him to. That's the tragedy: all that greatness, bent around one refusal. Even his name carries a story. In the tradition, he once tried to lift Shiva's mountain, Kailasa, and Shiva pressed it down with one toe, pinning him. Ravana roared so loudly the worlds shook, and Shiva, in the Uttara Kanda's telling, named him Ravana: the one who made the worlds cry out. Now the fight. Rama cuts off one of Ravana's heads with an arrow, and another grows back in its place. He cuts another. It grows back. Over and over. Some teachers read the ten heads as the things that keep growing back in all of us: desire, anger, greed, delusion, pride, jealousy, and the rest. Lists differ. The point doesn't. You can cut one down, and it comes back tomorrow. So this lesson doesn't ask you to kill all ten. It asks something smaller, and more honest: look at your own, pick one, and say its name.
screen: `SCHOLAR, DEVOTEE, MUSICIAN, KING.` · `THE ONE WHO MADE THE WORLDS CRY OUT.` · `CUT ONE HEAD. ANOTHER GROWS.` · `TEN HEADS: THE THINGS THAT GROW BACK.`

segments.voice: Picture ten heads without fear, and give them faces you might recognize: anger, wanting more, pride, jealousy, fear, laziness, the need to be right, whatever yours are. Pick the one that showed up most this week, look it in the face without fighting it, and say its name quietly, inside. When it grows back, and it will, you'll recognize it faster.
Ravana, the one who made the worlds cry out: the great, learned, ten-headed king, out of people to send, finally facing Rama himself.
Your line: name a head. Naming it is the first arrow. That's day sixty-five in the books.

howItsDone: At Dussehra, many communities in north India burn huge effigies of the ten-headed Ravana, and some teachers use the ten heads to speak about the inner faults that keep returning; the Shiva Tandava Stotram, attributed to Ravana, is chanted by devotees of Shiva.

original.note: Sanskrit: Ravana. The Uttara Kanda explains the name as 'the one who made the worlds cry out'.

trapdoor: what you thought: the ten-headed bad guy.
what it means: a great, learned king bent around one refusal, whose heads keep growing back like the faults we all carry.
what a scholar hears: the Uttara Kanda has Shiva name him Ravana after his roar under Kailasa; his older name is Dashagriva, the ten-necked.

notes: Indrajit's death at Lakshmana's hands is mentioned in passing; the outline has no separate day for it.
The heads growing back: in Valmiki, Rama cuts Ravana's heads and they regrow (Yuddha Kanda, before Agastya's counsel); confirm.
The ten heads as inner faults (kama, krodha, lobha, moha, mada, matsarya, etc.) is a common devotional reading, not Valmiki's; stated as 'many teachers read'. Confirm.
The Shiva Tandava Stotram's attribution to Ravana is traditional; confirm the phrasing 'traditionally said to be his'.
Name: Uttara Kanda story of Kailasa; Dashagriva as his earlier name. Confirm.
